subject: estimating variance of change in density over time

messages.author: 556fc1d104e92e95
messages.subject: estimating variance of change in density over time
parts:
We have density estimates of foxes from point counts in several areas
over four years. We want to estimate uncertainty around the estimates of
change in density between years for each area. The detection function
for each area was generated from data pooled over the four years.
Therefore, because the annual estimates are not independent, we think we
need to use equation 3.109 in the 2001 book to calculate the variance of
this change in densities.

The issues are: for any given survey period, we carried out repeat
surveys of the points, with variable effort at each point, therefore we
need to use equation 3.79 to calculate var n. To this by hand will be
laborious given the number of areas and years involved in our survey.
Does Distance output estimates of var n? If we have to do it by hand,
can we simply calculate var n from the variance of the encounter rate,
by multiplying this with the number of points surveyed?

Gavin

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: estimating variance of change in density over time
parts:
Hi Gavin, list,

If you pool the detection function across years, then comparing the density
estimates is the same as comparing the encounter rates, so you don't need to
worry about 3.109. You will need the var(n)s or var(n/L)s by year though.
Distance gives you n/L and %CV(n/L) on the Estiamtion Summary - Encounter
rates page of results. From this you can work out var(n/L) as
(n/L*CV(n/L))^2. Since in your case the effort varies by year, you're better
working with the n/Ls than the n's for making your comparison.

Were you going to do pairwise t-tests between all pairs of years to look for
changes (yikes!), or just adjacent years, or do some kind of trend analysis?
If the latter, see Chapter 5 of the ADS book. Simplest would be a linear
regression; if the var(n/L) between years are very different you could weight
by 1/var.

If you think there is some chance that detection probability did vary by year,
but that you don't have enough observations to fit a separate detection
function to each year of data, you could try fitting year as a factor
covariate using the MCDS engine (, or even a non-factor covariate to look for
a linear change in detectability over time -- or you could go further and have
a field for year^2, etc etc).

Hope this helps,

- Len
